{{Short description|Restriction on topological groups in mathematics}}
In mathematics, especially in [[topology]], a [[topological group]] <math>G</math> is said to have '''no small subgroup''' if there exists a [[neighbourhood (topology)|neighborhood]] <math>U</math> of the identity that contains no [[Trivial subgroup|nontrivial subgroup]] of <math>G.</math> An abbreviation '"'''NSS'''"' is sometimes used. A basic example of a topological group with no small subgroup is the [[general linear group]] over the complex numbers.

A [[locally compact]], [[separable metric space|separable metric]], [[Locally connected space|locally connected]] group with no small subgroup is a [[Lie group]]. (cf. [[Hilbert's fifth problem]].)
